Could Robert Pattinson get his first Oscar nomination for ‘Primetime’?

Robert Pattinson is already getting early Best Actor awards buzz for his portrayal of Chris Hansen in A24’s Primetime.

The movie goes back to the mid-2000s, when To Catch a Predator turned Hansen into one of television’s most recognizable faces.

The Dateline NBC series ran from 2004 to 2007, with Hansen confronting men caught in undercover investigations after communicating online with people they believed were teenagers. The show became hugely popular, but also raised questions about turning investigations and arrests into entertainment.

One major controversy came in 2006, when Texas assistant district attorney Bill Conradt was targeted in a sting. Conradt never went to the sting house. Police instead went to his home with a warrant, accompanied by an NBC camera crew, and he d!ed by su!c!de. His estate later sued NBC, and the case was settled.

NBC aired its final Predator investigation in December 2007 and retired the franchise soon after. Hansen has said the show simply ran its course, though the Conradt controversy remained associated with its ending.

Nearly 20 years later, Primetime revisits that world — but Hansen says this isn’t his version of the story.

He wasn’t involved in the movie and says he learned about it only after production had begun. He has also said several conversations and events shown in the film never happened. Speaking with Dan Abrams, Hansen questioned scenes involving his colleagues and producers and criticized the film for creating a fictionalized version without consulting the people who lived through it.

Hansen also walked out of a private screening after refusing an agreement concerning his name, image and likeness. He told the Los Angeles Times that he wants the film more clearly identified as fiction.

Pattinson, meanwhile, has called playing Hansen the most work he’s ever done and said he was “genuinely throwing up” from nerves before the Venice premiere.

So Primetime sits between real history and fictionalized drama — and Hansen’s disagreement makes the story behind it almost as interesting as the movie itself.
